cells.why: A `persisted` write is on disk at a majority before the answer, which is Raft's own commit rule. On etcd's spec no committed entry was lost with crashes, a lost disk (E-14c) or one damaged replica under `rejoin` (E-37, 27,985 states). E-29's journal of the same shape lost 0 of 10,020 acknowledged batches in 2,640 LazyFS power cuts; the sweeps on the real kernel are phase 2.
cells.why2: A `persisted` answer waits for the journal fsync on a majority of voters, and Raft keeps every committed entry: TLC on etcd's spec lost none through crashes and a lost disk replaced under a new id (E-14c), nor with one bad entry under `rejoin` (E-37), and no acknowledged write is lost across a move on E-17's harness. A journal of L0's shape lost 0 of 10,020 acknowledged batches in 2,640 LazyFS power cuts (E-29). So it holds by construction; the phase-2 sweeps on the real kernel are still owed.

cells.why: Judge 1's verdict stands, for its second reason only. Judge 2 is right that one bad entry is F-22's fault, not F-01's (F-10 says so), and that Raft's commit rule keeps a synced entry (E-14c, by reasoning for raft-rs). But F-01 also needs the store to give back after a power cut what it synced: E-29's journal lost an acknowledged batch in 2 of 1,200 rounds through a recovery bug, though it synced before it answered. PD's store is an LSM and no experiment ran it (AMENDMENTS 2, S: '`lsm`: no experiment'); both judges hold F-20 open for PD on the same ground.
cells.closes: a LazyFS power-loss run on an LSM store with PD's sync settings; none is planned

cells.why: Its commit is the in-sync set under an outside controller. No experiment modelled that composition, so there is no lost-write check for it.
cells.closes: a model of the in-sync set and controller rules with crashes and disk loss, then the 1,000-seed sim sweeps with crashes and power loss, and LazyFS on the real journal (phase 2)
cells.why2: A commit here is 'every member of the in-sync set' under a controller, not a majority of voters. This study never modelled or ran the in-sync set, its epochs or its recovery after a power loss of every machine.

cells.why: Its commit is a write quorum of log nodes, changed by a seal and a metadata CAS. That protocol was not modelled here (SPACE counts 3 to 4 novel mechanisms in it).
cells.closes: a model of the seal and CAS with crashes and disk loss, then the 1,000-seed sim sweeps with crashes and power loss, and LazyFS on the real journal (phase 2)
cells.why2: A write quorum of log nodes holds each write, and a seal with a metadata compare-and-swap changes the set. SPACE counts 3 to 4 novel mechanisms there, and no experiment modelled them.

cells.why: An acknowledged write is a finished PUT, so the machines hold nothing that must survive. But the manifest CAS and the lease that order the PUTs were only timed (E-28), never modelled.
cells.closes: a model of the manifest CAS and writer lease
cells.why2: A commit is a conditional PUT, so its bytes are as safe as the object store. But the manifest compare-and-swap and the writer lease that tie an answer to a PUT were only timed (E-28), never modelled.

cells.why: Judge 2 is right; I confirmed it in v4's own sim (sim/scale-probes.test.ts, 'short lane (durable)', pinned red today; STATUS.md). Step 1: n02 writes row x and leaves; n01 removes x and then writes 100 rows of its own. Step 2: tombstone GC and compaction drop the remove from n01's lane, but n02's old write stays the last entry of its lane on every disk. Step 3: n01 restarts from its own disk and shows x again. So an acknowledged remove does not survive a restart, and v4 takes no fix (AMENDMENTS 3). Judge 1 looked only at the stranded commit.

cells.why: Each dedup option held ONCE and REFUSED in E-20's exhaustive model under lost answers, a failover and a move in mid-retry (`sess` 13 rules, 14 under `fwd`; `win` 17 and 19). Porcupine and Knossos pass on the prototype's histories with A-04's refusal wait, and A-05's marks keep derived outputs once past the horizon (E-30).
cells.why2: Every dedup option holds 'no attempt twice' and 'a refused attempt never commits later' in every state of E-20's model: lost answers, a failover or a move mid-retry, a restart, expiry, with `forward.once` under `fwd`. Porcupine and real Knossos pass every partition history once a refusal waits for its commit (A-04), and `srchi-slot` marks keep derived outputs once past the horizon (A-05, E-30). Keyed method re-runs are reasoned, not modelled.

cells.why2: Its dedup is transaction ids under two-phase commit (Percolator), which is published but was not modelled here (E-20 ran `win`, `sess`, `pid` and `keys`). fero's attempts, refusals and retries on top of it were never written.

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. E-20's world is three abstract Raft groups: a crash deposes a leader and the new one keeps the committed log. `pid` holds there with A-22's two fixes (16 rules). ISR's own leader change (the in-sync set, leader epochs, a controller) was never modelled, and both judges hold F-01 and F-03 open for ISR for that reason. An attempt cannot be shown to land once across a failover that is itself not shown; judge 2 left the default.
cells.closes: a model of the in-sync-set leader change under E-20's scenarios; none is planned

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. `win` holds in E-20's model (17 rules, 19 under `fwd`), whose groups are Raft. SLOG changes writers by a seal and a metadata compare-and-swap, never modelled; a late append by the old writer is the case that matters. Both judges hold F-01 and F-03 open for SLOG on this; judge 2 left the default.
cells.closes: a model of the seal and writer change under E-20's scenarios; none is planned

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. `sess` holds in E-20's model, whose groups are Raft. OBJ changes writers by a lease and a compare-and-swap on the manifest, which no experiment modelled (E-28 timed the PUT only), and both judges hold F-03 open for OBJ. E-20's own line moves OBJ up on F-02; it does not show it. Judge 2 left the default.
cells.closes: a model of the lease and manifest compare-and-swap under E-20's scenarios, with a paused old writer; none is planned

cells.why: v4's own scoped sweep pins it (STATUS.md, KNOWN_UNSAFE, A2 seed 9). Step by step: a forwarded write commits at the owner; a cut strands that commit; the issuer retries; the new owner commits it again; both stand after the heal. A write issued from a tap is also committed twice.
cells.why2: STATUS.md pins it in v4's own sim (sim/scoped-sweep.test.ts, KNOWN_UNSAFE, A2 seed 9). Step 1: a forwarded write commits at its owner, and the owner is cut off before the commit leaves it. Step 2: the issuer retries and the new owner commits it again. Step 3: after the heal both commits stand. A write issued from a tap during a commit is also committed twice.

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. E-20's rules hold for SIDE's writes (`sess`, 14 rules under `fwd`). But SIDE runs each call at its partition's leader (U `ldr`), and SPACE counts one novel rule there: calls in flight across a handover. No experiment modelled it: E-20 reasons about a re-run as a late resend, and E-22 ran calls at the writer across a failover only to judge check-then-set. cells.closes: an E-20-style model of a call in flight across a handover under U `ldr`; none is planned

cells.why: Measured on JetStream: a retry lands twice once the dedup window has passed, and an `incr` retried after one other write to the row was counted again (3 where 2 was right). The attempt id lives only in the row's last message, and fero cannot change the log.
cells.why2: On JetStream a retried attempt lands twice once the dedup window has passed, and an `incr` whose answer was lost was counted again after one other write to the row: the counter read 3 where 2 was right (E-44). The message id must name one try, not the attempt, or a refused publish burns it (58 of 200 increments lost).

cells.why: Each dedup option held ONCE and REFUSED in E-20's exhaustive model under lost answers, a failover and a move in mid-retry (`sess` 13 rules, 14 under `fwd`; `win` 17 and 19). Porcupine and Knossos pass on the prototype's histories with A-04's refusal wait, and A-05's marks keep derived outputs once past the horizon (E-30).
cells.why2: Every dedup option holds 'no attempt twice' and 'a refused attempt never commits later' in every state of E-20's model: lost answers, a failover or a move mid-retry, a restart, expiry, with `forward.once` under `fwd`. Porcupine and real Knossos pass every partition history once a refusal waits for its commit (A-04), and `srchi-slot` marks keep derived outputs once past the horizon (A-05, E-30). Keyed method re-runs are reasoned, not modelled.

cells.why: Judge 1's verdict stands, but on steps I confirmed in v4's code, not on its steps 2 and 3 (STATUS.md says a minority is read-only, and the stranded commit is one writer after another). Step 1: v4's own monitor asks for one writer per partition per epoch only, and exempts epoch 0 by design: 'open genesis is multi-writer LWW' (sim/monitors.ts). Step 2: an owner commits alone, before any other member holds the write, whenever its own link table shows a majority (kernel/membership.ts `gate`; STATUS.md: 'no other node ever held the first commit'). Step 3: so no lease and no majority round orders an old owner's last commit before the new owner's first one once the others vote it out. So more than one writer can commit to a partition at a time; judge 2's 'one owner per view' is true per view only.

cells.why: Lease reads over multi-version state are published (TiKV), but nothing here modelled them, and W `lease` needs bounded clock drift.
cells.closes: a model or a checker run of its read path; none is planned
cells.why2: Reads go by leader leases and MVCC timestamps. `lease` needs bounded clock drift and was not tested here (G-25).

cells.why: A reader is safe only below the high watermark, which rests on leader epochs across a failover. That part was not modelled; E-31 covers the protocol above a correct log.
cells.closes: a model of the high watermark across an ISR leader change
cells.why2: Readers stop at the high watermark, and Kafka's KIP-320 detects a truncated log. E-31 did not model the in-sync set's truncation on a leader change, and does not name this row.

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. E-31's model takes the committed log as given: a group with a leader and a follower, where a crash loses only the uncommitted tail. SLOG's own log, a write quorum of log nodes changed by a seal and a metadata compare-and-swap, was never modelled, and both judges hold F-01 open for SLOG. A reader's view cannot be shown to be a prefix of a committed log that is itself not shown; judge 2 held ISR and OBJ open on this ground and left SLOG at the default.
cells.closes: a model of the seal and compare-and-swap that says which entries a reader may be served, then E-31's bounds on it; none is planned

cells.why: State reads use a time lease at the writer (W `lease`), which no experiment tested, and the lease and manifest CAS were not modelled.
cells.closes: a model of the lease reads and the manifest CAS
cells.why2: State reads go by a leader lease, which needs bounded clock drift and was never tested (G-25). The commit-by-PUT path under a paused writer was not modelled.

cells.why: Judge 2 is right; I confirmed it in sim/scale-probes.test.ts ('zombie lane', pinned red today; STATUS.md). Step 1: n04 commits x = v2 as its links sever, and is voted out. Step 2: n01 removes x at epoch 2; readers on n01, n02 and n03 see it gone, and the three collect the tombstone. Step 3: the link heals, the three take n04's older write and show v2 again, while n04, which showed v2, shows nothing. So readers saw a write that later disappeared, on both sides. Judge 1 held it open because no run in this study judged it; v4's own pinned test does.

cells.why: A crash needs the controller to pick a new leader from the in-sync set, which SPACE names as a delay. No failover or handover was timed for this family.
cells.closes: pins on three processes of an ISR prototype
cells.why2: A controller picks the new leader from the in-sync set after a session timeout, and SPACE notes that a controller election delays it. Neither a failover nor a handover was timed here (E-09c ran Kafka for speed only).

cells.why: A writer change is a seal plus a metadata CAS plus a new writer. None of it was timed here.
cells.closes: pins on three processes of a log-first prototype
cells.why2: The controller changes writers by a seal and a compare-and-swap. No experiment timed a writer's crash or a planned change.

cells.why: A handover is one CAS on the manifest: 1.4 ms p50 on MinIO here, but about 30 ms on a real store (cited), which is over 10 ms. Failover waits for the lease to end and needs the warm standby (A-26, reasoned).
cells.closes: pins against a real object store
cells.why2: A handover or a failover is at least one conditional PUT on the manifest, plus the lease wait: 2.7 ms at p99 on MinIO here, about 30 ms typical on S3 Standard (cited in E-28), which is over the 10 ms handover bar on a real store. The lease-based failover was not timed.

cells.why: v4 has no leader to fail over. How long a partition is unwritable after its owner crashes was not measured in this study.
cells.closes: a pin on v4; not planned
cells.why2: DESIGN-V5 4.2 puts v4's eviction at about 4 s by default ('2 s is still half of v4's eviction'), over the 2.5 s bar. It is a setting (`heartbeat.ms`), and nothing in this study timed v4.

cells.why: With writer time as the median (A-23) a leader's clock jump caused 0 failovers in 60 simulated runs, and a kernel on a worker kept its heartbeat within 5 ms through main-thread pauses (E-07). But A-02's CheckQuorum every E/4 (500 ms at E = 2 s) was never run with pauses up to 1 s on kernel threads (K-28), and the median was simulated with three or five clocks only: with one or two clocks a skewed clock is not outvoted (K-11, reasoned only).
cells.closes: the phase-2 sim: pauses up to 1 s on kernel threads with CheckQuorum at E/4 (K-28), and the median with one or two clocks and a changing member set (K-11)
cells.why2: The kernel on its own thread kept its heartbeat within 5 ms through a 5 s main-thread stall and 0.3 to 0.5 s GCs (E-07), and the median clock rule (A-23) cost no failover in the 60 runs where the leader's clock jumped and ended no row more than 100 ms early (E-21, simulated, three and five clocks). Not run: CheckQuorum every E/4 (500 ms at E = 2 s) against pauses of up to 1 s on kernel threads (K-28), and groups with fewer than three clocks (K-11). Read literally (E-21's reading), the first clause changes no row here: no row holds T `hlc`.

cells.why: STATUS.md: after every member stops cleanly one at a time, only the last to stop can bring the cluster back. Step by step: each leaver's dir holds the view it saw last, one it is not in; so the first two back sit `joining` until the last returns; no kernel rule can re-form them safely. v4's own `stopsOneByOne` harness pins it on the sim and on real sockets, and the ledger marks it decided, not changed.
cells.why2: STATUS.md, pinned in sim/leave-harness.ts (`stopsOneByOne`) and tests/stops.test.ts. Step 1: each clean leaver's dir holds the last view it saw, a view it is not in. Step 2: the last view's only voter is the last to stop. Step 3: so the first two back sit `joining` until that one returns, and no kernel rule can re-form them safely.

cells.why: State is a fold of one ordered log per partition, so a rejoin or a collection replays the remove in order, and v4's lane bugs cannot arise (reasoned). But no experiment ran it: E-33 left erasure out of its restore model, and a seed beside a restored or moved partition was not modelled.
cells.closes: the phase-2 sim monitor with v4's two row-comes-back bugs as seeds, and a restore model with removes
cells.why2: With one ordered log per partition a remove is an entry that every copy folds, and E-31's model shows no ghost row at a subscriber across a failover, a reload, a move and a relay. But E-33 left erasure out of its restore model, and snapshot layers against retention (the tier's one mechanism) were never modelled, which is the kind of place where v4's rows came back.

cells.why: STATUS.md pins it red today. Step by step: one node writes a row and leaves; another removes it; tombstone GC and compaction drop the remove from the remover's lane; the old write is still the last entry of the leaver's lane; so a joiner, and a member back from its own disk, bring the row back.
cells.why2: STATUS.md pins three ways in v4's own tests. One: after tombstone GC and compaction a removed row comes back from a short lane (sim/scale-probes.test.ts). Two: a write from an evicted member beats a newer remove after a heal. Three: a fresh member's `data:` seed brings back a deleted seed row (2 runs of 2).

cells.why: Two machines plus any third voter is a three-voter Raft group. On etcd's spec three voters with one crash break no invariant and have no stuck state (E-14b), etcd took writes again after a kill -9 of its leader with every retried write acknowledged (E-13), and the port was linearizable on 3 nodes (E-46). The health line for two voters alone is a phase-2 test.
cells.why2: Three voters on three failure domains is plain Raft: either machine's crash leaves a majority of two, and every acknowledged write is on two of the three disks; a small full server counts as the third voter, so no witness rule is needed. A failover on three members was measured on etcd (E-13), and RLOG's writer change holds in E-16's model. Without a third voter the draft keeps one voter and words the health line (DESIGN-V5 4.2); that line is design, not a test.

cells.why: Judge 2 is right. cells.why: The kernel runs on a worker (M `kw`, A-27). Through a 5 s main-thread stall it kept its heartbeat within 5 ms and write p99 at or under 4 ms, where a main-thread kernel went silent for 2.6 to 5.1 s (E-07). A throw on the main thread cannot reach the kernel's thread; writer rules run on the kernel thread under a time budget, whose cost is a phase-2 pin.
cells.why2: With the kernel on its own thread (M `kw`), a prototype kept its heartbeat within 5 ms of schedule and write p99 at or under 4 ms through a 5 s main-thread stall and forced GCs of 0.3 to 0.5 s; on the main thread it went silent for 2.6 to 5.1 s (E-07). The seam carries byte batches and the worker keeps its row index off the V8 heap (A-27), since E-34 measured pauses of 0.25 to 0.49 s with it on. A throw goes to the reporter as in V4-47 (design; those tests are not ported yet).

cells.why: Step by step: (1) v4 runs kernel, fold and user code on one event loop (M `loop`). (2) A synchronous stall in user code blocks that loop, so the kernel sends no heartbeat and no acknowledgement. (3) E-07 measured it: a main-thread kernel went silent for 2.6 to 5.1 s in a 5 s stall, past any 2 s election time.
cells.why2: Step 1: v4 runs the kernel, the fold and user code on one event loop (M `loop`). Step 2: a stalled loop sends no heartbeat and answers no write. Step 3: E-07's control, the same kernel on the main thread, went silent for 5.1 s in a 5 s stall and 2.6 s under forced GCs, with write p99 4.9 s. So a stalled main thread stalls replication and failure detection.

cells.why: Replication and failure detection sit in the native daemon, so a stalled app cannot stop them. But L2 runs in the app's Node process for the groups its host leads, so whether writes go on through a 5 s stall there was not shown.

cells.why: This row founds by `fero init` and requires no store across boxes, so the home of the restore mark is not decided (A-08, G-21). If it is the store's manifest, the clash of AMENDMENTS 1.3's F-15 line applies: a slot move would wait. No run had the store down.
cells.closes: a sim with the store down for 1 h (phase 3; K-21, K-23), once the mark has a home
cells.why2: AMENDMENTS 1.3, F-15: this row requires no object store, and A-08 leaves the home of its restore mark open, so the clash (a move waits for the store) is not shown for it. Writes and failover use local journals only, by design; no sim ran with the store down.

cells.why: AMENDMENTS 1.3, F-15's line. Step by step: A-08 records every new slot epoch in the store's manifest before it is used (E-33, a needed rule); a slot move raises the epoch; so a slot move waits while the store is down; and F-15 lets only wake, new replicas and old history wait. Writes and failover do not wait. With slot moves added to the list it is open: the store was always reachable in E-33's model.
cells.closes: a sim with the store down for 1 h (phase 3; K-21, K-23)

cells.why2: Healing with full voters and learners is model-checked (E-16, E-14c). But this row's log replicas join healing when servers are short and 'lead only to repair' (DESIGN-V5 4.2), and E-16 left witnesses out (G-25).

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. The rejoin is shown only in part: E-16's model cuts members off and heals them with no operator step (4 members, up to two faults, both healing options live), but its Raft is abstract and catch-up is one step; E-14c runs etcd's own spec, leaves out 'partitions as such', and its full runs did not finish (G-10). The second half is not shown: after a long cut the leader's log is gone and the draft sends a snapshot 'as any new replica does' (DESIGN-V5 4.2), a whole copy (5.2 to 6.9 s per GB on etcd, E-13), not only what the member lacks. Judge 2 called that fallback met by construction.
cells.closes: the phase-2 sim's partitions from 10 s to 1 h on the real kernel, with retention and snapshot catch-up, and a pin on the bytes a member copies when it is back after the log was cut

cells.why: AMENDMENTS 1.3, F-17's line: 5 of 280 five-node partial partitions stayed stuck for good with a connected majority, on etcd's own raft code. It is Raft's vote rule (the only well-connected server has a shorter log), and the row takes no new election rule. Restated to a majority that holds an up-to-date replica it is open: CheckQuorum every E/4 gave 1.52 E at worst on the named cases only, and the sweeps were not rerun with it.
cells.closes: the 3- and 5-node sweeps, and one real-TCP run, with A-02's constants (CheckQuorum at E/4, 0.25 E jitter)
cells.why2: AMENDMENTS 1.3, F-17: 5 of 280 five-node partial partitions stayed stuck for good with a connected majority, because the one server linked to a majority had a shorter log and Raft's vote rule refused it (E-38, simulated on etcd's own raft code; none with three nodes). Restated to 'a connected majority that includes an up-to-date replica' it is open: nothing flapped, but 62 of 280 runs took 3.0 to 3.9 E with etcd's timers, and CheckQuorum every E/4 (A-02) was run on the named cases only (1.52 E at worst).

cells.why: E-29(b) is the acceptance test, and it passes on tmpfs and ext4 with A-09's six format rules: writes refused `disk-full` with a retry-after; removes, 200 term changes, a member change, a snapshot and a retention pass done while full; 3,000 of 3,000 writes taken once space was back. A full follower stopped acknowledging, said so, and caught up by itself in 348 ms. A real election and a handover on a full disk were not run.
cells.why2: E-29 ran F-20's own test on a journal of L0's shape and on a three-process pipeline, on 64 MB tmpfs and ext4. The 80 % line printed once; at the hard limit data writes were refused `disk-full` with a retry-after while reads, 500 removes, 200 term changes, a member change, a snapshot and a retention pass went on from the reserve; a full follower stopped acknowledging, said so, and caught up by itself in 348 to 513 ms. A-09's six format rules are what make it hold; an election on a full disk was sized (56 B a vote), not run.

Judge 1 named the same facts and stopped at open.

cells.why: Z `rejoin` (A-28): a checksum per entry turns damage into a wipe, and the wiped replica never votes under its old id. On etcd's spec with three voters and one damaged entry all 10 invariants hold and 0 of 1,178 judged states are stuck (27,985 states); without either rule a committed write is lost in 32 states. Whether one bad entry wipes one group or the whole journal is K-24.
cells.why2: With Z `rejoin` a checksum per entry finds the bad entry, and the replica wipes itself and returns as a new one that never votes under its old id. TLC on etcd's spec explored all 27,985 states: all 10 invariants hold, no committed write is lost, and no judged state is stuck (E-37). Both rules are needed: without the checksum a committed write is lost with one fault, in 32 states.
